lessons.title: Math is Everywhere
lessons.objective: I can find applications of math outside of school — in professions like being a chef, in hobbies like gardening, and around my own house.
lessons.languageObjective: I can describe how someone uses math at work using the words plan, calculate, and measure.

concept.heading: Math is an integral part of nearly every profession
concept.intro: Chefs supervise a team of cooks preparing everything from appetizers to desserts. Watch how much of that job is quietly mathematical.
concept.keyIdea: Mathematical Modeling in Careers & Daily Life. 1. Frame real-world problems mathematically using rates, percentages, and geometry. 2. Collect and analyze data to optimize decisions and resource allocation. 3. Communicate quantitative findings clearly with equations and visual models

worked.title: Watch me find the math in a chef's day
lines: When chefs plan menus, they determine the number of items on the menu and calculate the price point for each item.
They decide on the portion size of each item and project how much food is needed for each day.
They calculate how much of each ingredient to order — that is counting, measuring, and multiplying, all before a single dish is cooked.
linesEs: Cuando los chefs planean los menús, determinan cuántos platillos habrá y calculan el precio de cada uno.
Deciden el tamaño de la porción de cada platillo y proyectan cuánta comida hace falta para cada día.
Calculan cuánto pedir de cada ingrediente — eso es contar, medir y multiplicar, todo antes de cocinar un solo platillo.
worked.titleEs: Mírame hallar las matemáticas en el día de un chef

together.title: Let's find the math in a garden together
lines: A planter that is 4 feet long and 2 feet wide has an area of 4 × 2 = 8 square feet — that tells us how many plants fit.
If the soil needs to be 1 foot deep, the volume is 4 × 2 × 1 = 8 cubic feet — that tells us how much soil to buy.
Gardeners also measure seed depth and the distance between seeds. What other garden decisions need math?
linesEs: Una jardinera de 4 pies de largo y 2 pies de ancho tiene un área de 4 × 2 = 8 pies cuadrados — eso nos dice cuántas plantas caben.
Si la tierra debe tener 1 pie de profundidad, el volumen es 4 × 2 × 1 = 8 pies cúbicos — eso nos dice cuánta tierra comprar.
Los jardineros también miden la profundidad de las semillas y la distancia entre ellas. ¿Qué otras decisiones del jardín necesitan matemáticas?
together.titleEs: Hallemos juntos las matemáticas en un jardín

vocabulary.definition: A job someone is trained to do, like chef, nurse, or carpenter.
vocabulary.example: A chef prices a menu; a nurse measures a dose; a carpenter cuts to length.

vocabulary.definition: The supply of items a business keeps on hand, tracked by counting.
vocabulary.example: The kitchen counts 40 lb of flour and 12 dozen eggs on hand.

vocabulary.definition: The measured amount of food served to one person.
vocabulary.example: Each bowl of soup uses 2 cups of broth — one person's serving.

vocabulary.definition: The amount of flat space a surface covers, measured in square units.
vocabulary.example: A 4 ft by 2 ft planter covers 8 square feet of ground.

vocabulary.definition: The amount of space something fills, measured in cubic units.
vocabulary.example: 4 ft × 2 ft × 1 ft of soil = 8 cubic feet.

lessons.title: Math is Beauty
lessons.objective: I can use bilateral symmetry to describe structure in nature and in human creations.
lessons.languageObjective: I can describe a symmetric design using the words mirror image, line of symmetry, and balance.

concept.heading: Math creates beautiful designs in nature
concept.intro: Look closely at a butterfly's wings, then at how a plant grows its leaves. The same mathematical idea keeps appearing.
concept.keyIdea: Symmetry, Geometry & Design. 1. Line of Symmetry: Divides a figure into two congruent mirror-image halves. 2. Rotational Symmetry: Shape rotates onto itself in less than a full 360° turn. 3. Geometric transformations preserve angle measures and side lengths

worked.title: Watch me find the symmetry in a butterfly
lines: I look at the two sides of the butterfly, and they look like mirror images — the butterfly is symmetric.
All butterflies have reflective symmetry. In plants and animals, this is called bilateral symmetry.
To show it, I draw a line down the middle of the butterfly's body: everything on the left is reflected on the right.
linesEs: Miro los dos lados de la mariposa y se ven como imágenes en espejo — la mariposa es simétrica.
Todas las mariposas tienen simetría de reflexión. En plantas y animales, a esto se le llama simetría bilateral.
Para mostrarla, trazo una línea por en medio del cuerpo de la mariposa: todo lo que está a la izquierda se refleja a la derecha.
worked.titleEs: Mírame hallar la simetría en una mariposa

together.title: Let's find the symmetry in a growing plant
lines: This plant grows in layers, and each layer is made up of two leaves — so 3 layers hold 3 × 2 = 6 leaves.
In the first layer, one leaf is a mirror image of the other.
To show the bilateral symmetry in the second layer, we draw a line down the middle of the layer, along the center of each leaf.
Are the leaves EXACTLY symmetric? Nature comes close, but living things are never perfectly identical.
linesEs: Esta planta crece por capas, y cada capa está formada por dos hojas — así que 3 capas tienen 3 × 2 = 6 hojas.
En la primera capa, una hoja es la imagen en espejo de la otra.
Para mostrar la simetría bilateral en la segunda capa, trazamos una línea por en medio de la capa, por el centro de cada hoja.
¿Las hojas son exactamente simétricas? La naturaleza se acerca mucho, pero los seres vivos nunca son perfectamente idénticos.
together.titleEs: Hallemos la simetría en una planta que crece

vocabulary.definition: Having two halves that match — one side is a mirror image of the other.
vocabulary.example: A butterfly: the left wing is the mirror of the right.

vocabulary.definition: A copy of a figure flipped across a line, so the two halves face each other.
vocabulary.example: Fold the layer down the middle: each leaf lands on its partner.

vocabulary.definition: Reflective symmetry in plants and animals — the two sides of the body mirror each other.
vocabulary.example: All 17,000+ butterfly species have it — two sides, one mirror line.

vocabulary.definition: The line you can draw through a figure so each side is a reflection of the other.
vocabulary.example: The line straight down the butterfly's body.

vocabulary.definition: An even, steady arrangement — neither side feels heavier than the other.
vocabulary.example: Two matching halves — neither side feels heavier than the other.

title: Symmetry Safari
mission: Look for mathematical structure in nature and design. Test symmetry with evidence and connect observations to a precise representation.
investigate: Plot mirror partners on either side of the y-axis.
Add a point on the mirror line. Why does its reflection stay in place?
Explain the difference between an ideal symmetric model and an almost-symmetric natural object.
create: Design an emblem inspired by nature. Give at least three mirror pairs on a coordinate grid and explain where its symmetry is exact and where a real example may differ.

support.prompt: A planter is 4 feet long and 2 feet wide. What is its area?
support.explanation: Area of a rectangle is length × width: 4 × 2 = 8 square feet.
feedback: 2 comes from dividing 4 by 2 instead of multiplying.
6 comes from adding 4 + 2 instead of multiplying.
12 comes from adding all four sides (4 + 2 + 4 + 2) — that is the perimeter, not the area.
hints: Area tells how much flat space the planter covers.
For a rectangle, multiply length by width.
Multiply 4 × 2.

support.prompt: That same planter is 4 feet long, 2 feet wide, and needs soil 1 foot deep. How much soil does the gardener need?
support.explanation: Volume is length × width × depth: 4 × 2 × 1 = 8 cubic feet of soil.
feedback: 4 forgets to multiply by the width of 2.
7 comes from adding 4 + 2 + 1 instead of multiplying.
The number is right but soil fills space, so volume needs cubic units, not square units.
hints: Soil fills space, so you need volume.
Volume of a box is length × width × depth.
Multiply 4 × 2 × 1.

support.prompt: Leaving the water running while brushing wastes an average of 4 gallons per brushing. You brush twice a day. How much water can one person save per day by only turning the water on to rinse?
support.explanation: 4 gallons saved per brushing × 2 brushings a day = 8 gallons a day.
feedback: 2 comes from dividing 4 by 2 instead of multiplying.
4 gallons is the savings for only ONE brushing — you brush twice a day.
6 comes from adding 4 + 2 instead of multiplying.
hints: How many gallons does one brushing save?
How many times do you brush each day?
Multiply 4 × 2.

support.prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the ways chefs use math when planning menus?
choices: Calculating the price point for each item
Deciding on the portion size of each item
Projecting how much food is needed for each day
Choosing the color of the restaurant's walls
support.explanation: Price points, portion sizes, and food projections are all menu-planning math. Wall color is a design choice, not a menu calculation.
feedback: Calculating a price point is one of the menu-planning tasks the lesson listed — it IS math a chef does.
Deciding portion size is one of the menu-planning tasks the lesson listed — it IS math a chef does.
Projecting how much food is needed each day is one of the menu-planning tasks the lesson listed — it IS math a chef does.
hints: Three of these came straight from the list of menu-planning math.
Which one has no calculating, measuring, or projecting in it?
Which one is about looks, not amounts?

support.prompt: Name one task a chef does that uses math, and say what math is inside it.
support.frame: A chef uses math when they ___ .
support.explanation: A chef sets the price for each dish. That uses math because the chef has to calculate what the ingredients cost and add enough to make a profit.

support.prompt: What does it mean that a butterfly is symmetric?
choices: The butterfly has exactly two wings
The two sides of the butterfly look like mirror images
The butterfly's wings are very colorful
The butterfly is larger than most insects
support.explanation: Symmetric means one side is a mirror image of the other — that is exactly what we see across the butterfly's body.
feedback: Having two wings is not enough — the two sides must MIRROR each other to be symmetric.
Color makes a butterfly pretty, but symmetry is about the two sides matching, not about color.
Size has nothing to do with symmetry — a tiny butterfly is just as symmetric as a big one.
hints: Think about what you see on the left wing versus the right wing.
Imagine a mirror standing along the butterfly's body.
What word describes two sides that reflect each other?

support.prompt: In plants and animals, reflective symmetry is called:
support.explanation: The lesson says it directly: all butterflies have reflective symmetry, and in plants and animals this is called bilateral symmetry.
feedback: Rotational symmetry is about turning a shape, not reflecting it across a line.
A mirror image is what each SIDE is — the name for the whole property in living things is different.
Balance is why our brains find symmetry pleasing, not the name of the symmetry itself.
hints: The word starts with 'bi-', meaning two.
It describes the two sides of a body.
Bi-lateral means two-sided.

support.prompt: A plant grows in layers, and each layer is made up of 2 leaves. How many leaves does the plant have after growing 4 layers?
feedback: 4 counts the layers but forgets each layer holds 2 leaves.
6 comes from adding 4 + 2 instead of multiplying.
16 doubles the layers first (4 × 2 = 8, then × 2 again) — each layer has 2 leaves, not 4.
hints: How many leaves are in ONE layer?
There are 4 equal layers.
Multiply 4 × 2.

support.prompt: How can you SHOW that a layer of two leaves has bilateral symmetry?
choices: Count the total number of leaves on the plant
Measure how tall the plant is
Draw a line down the middle of the layer and check that each side mirrors the other
Color the two leaves different colors
support.explanation: The lesson's method: draw a line down the middle of the layer, along the center of each leaf, and see that one side is a mirror image of the other.
feedback: Counting leaves tells you how many there are, not whether the two sides mirror each other.
Height says nothing about whether the left side reflects the right side.
Coloring them differently would actually BREAK the mirror-image match, not demonstrate it.
hints: Symmetry is about two sides matching.
You need something for the sides to reflect ACROSS.
What did we draw down the middle of the butterfly?

support.prompt: Where have you seen symmetry before? Name one place and describe it.
support.explanation: I have seen symmetry in my own face in the mirror — my left side and right side are almost mirror images of each other, with an eye and an ear on each side.

core.prompt: One person saves 8 gallons of water a day by turning the water on only to rinse. How much water does that person save in a year (365 days)?
core.explanation: 8 gallons a day × 365 days = 2,920 gallons in a year.
feedback: 365 is just the number of days; it forgets to multiply by the gallons saved each day.
373 comes from adding 8 + 365 instead of multiplying.
1,460 multiplies 365 by 4 — the savings from one brushing — instead of the full 8 gallons a day.
hints: You know the savings per day.
How many days are in a year?
Multiply 8 × 365.

core.prompt: If each person in a house saves 2,920 gallons a year, how much does a household of 3 people save in a year?
core.explanation: 2,920 gallons per person × 3 people = 8,760 gallons a year.
feedback: 973 (about 2,920 ÷ 3) divides instead of multiplying — more people save MORE water, not less.
2,923 comes from adding 2,920 + 3 instead of multiplying.
5,840 multiplies by 2 people instead of 3.
hints: Each person saves the same amount.
3 people, each saving 2,920 gallons.
Multiply 2,920 × 3.

core.prompt: A household of 5 saves 2,920 gallons per person per year. A household of 4 does the same. How much MORE does the household of 5 save than the household of 4?
core.explanation: 5 people save 5 × 2,920 = 14,600 gallons and 4 people save 4 × 2,920 = 11,680 gallons. The difference is 14,600 − 11,680 = 2,920 gallons — exactly one more person's savings.
feedback: 1 is just the difference in the number of people — each of those people saves 2,920 gallons.
11,680 is the TOTAL for the household of 4, not the difference between the two households.
14,600 is the TOTAL for the household of 5, not the difference between the two households.
hints: How many more people does the bigger household have?
One more person means one more person's yearly savings.
Each person saves 2,920 gallons a year.

core.prompt: A gardener's planter has an area of 8 square feet, and each plant needs 2 square feet of space to grow. How many plants fit in the planter?
core.explanation: 8 square feet ÷ 2 square feet per plant = 4 plants.
feedback: 6 comes from subtracting 8 − 2 instead of dividing.
10 comes from adding 8 + 2 instead of dividing.
16 multiplies 8 × 2 instead of dividing — that would need a much bigger planter.
hints: You are splitting the area into equal shares of space.
How many groups of 2 square feet fit inside 8 square feet?
Divide 8 by 2.

core.prompt: Choose another person who works in a restaurant — not the chef — and describe the math they would use.
core.frame: A ___ in a restaurant uses math when ___ .
core.explanation: A server uses math all shift. They add up each table's bill, calculate the change for customers paying cash, and figure out their tips as a percent of each check. At the end of the night they total their tips to see what they earned.

core.prompt: Why do people find symmetry pleasing?
choices: Our brains are wired to favor balance, and bilateral symmetry provides balance
Symmetric things are always brightly colored
Symmetry only appears in rare and expensive objects
Symmetric shapes are always larger than non-symmetric ones
core.explanation: The lesson says it directly: our brains are wired to favor balance, and bilateral symmetry provides balance.
feedback: Color is separate from symmetry — a plain gray moth can be perfectly symmetric.
Symmetry is everywhere in nature, from leaves to ladybugs — it is common, not rare.
Size has nothing to do with it — a tiny symmetric leaf is as balanced as a huge one.
hints: The answer is about how our brains respond.
What does bilateral symmetry provide that brains favor?
Think of an even, steady arrangement.

core.prompt: There are over 17,000 species of butterflies, and ALL butterflies have reflective symmetry. About how many of those species have reflective symmetry?
choices: None — symmetry is only in plants
core.explanation: 'All butterflies have reflective symmetry' means every one of the 17,000+ species — no exceptions.
feedback: 'All' means every single species, not half of them.
Symmetry is about the two sides matching, not about how colorful the wings are.
The butterfly itself was our first example — animals show bilateral symmetry too.
hints: Read the statement carefully: ALL butterflies.
Does 'all' leave any out?
Every species means every species.

core.prompt: A plant grows 2 leaves at a time, one layer per week. How many leaves has it grown after 6 weeks?
core.explanation: One layer per week for 6 weeks is 6 layers, and 6 layers × 2 leaves = 12 leaves.
feedback: 6 counts the layers but forgets each layer holds 2 leaves.
8 comes from adding 6 + 2 instead of multiplying.
36 squares the 6 weeks (6 × 6) instead of multiplying weeks by leaves per layer.
hints: How many layers grow in 6 weeks?
Each layer is made up of 2 leaves.
Multiply 6 × 2.

core.prompt: Which is the best test for whether a figure has bilateral symmetry?
choices: Check whether the figure has an even number of parts
Find a line where one side is the mirror image of the other
Check whether the figure is found in nature
Check whether the figure looks beautiful to you
core.explanation: Bilateral symmetry means exactly this: there is a line across which the two sides are mirror images.
feedback: An even number of parts is not enough — the letter Z has 2 matching ends but no mirror line.
Humans create bilateral symmetry too, in art, music, and architecture — nature is not required.
Beauty is an opinion; the mirror-image test gives the same answer no matter who runs it.
hints: Go back to the definition, not the feeling.
What must exist for the two sides to reflect across?
Mirror image across a line.

core.prompt: Are the two leaves in a real plant layer EXACTLY symmetric? Why might this be?
core.explanation: No — the leaves are close to mirror images but not exact. Real plants grow in messy conditions: one leaf might get more sun or get nibbled by an insect, so the two sides come out slightly different. Nature follows the pattern of bilateral symmetry without being perfect.

stretch.prompt: Each person saves 2,920 gallons a year. Which correctly compares households of 3, 4, 5, and 8 people?
feedback: Those add the household size to 2,920 instead of multiplying by it.
20,440 is 7 × 2,920 — the last household has 8 people, not 7.
46,720 is 16 × 2,920 — that doubles the 8-person household instead of computing it.
hints: Each household total is people × 2,920.
Check the last value most carefully.

stretch.prompt: A chef expects 120 customers tonight and projects that 1 out of every 4 will order the soup. Each serving of soup uses 2 cups of broth. How much broth should the chef prepare?
stretch.explanation: 120 ÷ 4 = 30 soup orders, and 30 orders × 2 cups each = 60 cups of broth.
feedback: 15 divides the 30 orders by 2 instead of multiplying by 2.
30 is the number of soup ORDERS; it forgets to multiply by the 2 cups each serving needs.
240 uses all 120 customers × 2 cups — but only 1 in 4 customers orders the soup.
hints: First find how many customers will order soup.
120 ÷ 4 = 30 orders.
Now, how many cups do 30 servings need?

stretch.prompt: Someone says, 'Math is just a school subject. I'll never use it after class.' Using the chef, the gardener, or the water problem, write what you would say back.
stretch.explanation: I would say that a chef never stops using math — they calculate prices, portion sizes, and how much of each ingredient to order every single day. Even at home, math showed us that one person who turns off the tap while brushing saves 2,920 gallons a year. You do not escape math after class; you just stop noticing you are using it.

stretch.prompt: Your friend insists that only ONE of two flowers has bilateral symmetry, but both pass the mirror-image test — just across lines pointing in different directions. What is the best response?
choices: Your friend is right, because a real line of symmetry must always be vertical
Both flowers have bilateral symmetry — a line of symmetry does not have to point the same direction in every figure
Neither flower has bilateral symmetry, because flowers are not animals
Agree with your friend, because two people should not disagree about math
stretch.explanation: The test for bilateral symmetry is whether SOME line makes the two sides mirror images — the direction of that line does not matter.
feedback: Nothing in the definition requires vertical — a mirror line can run in any direction.
Plants have bilateral symmetry too; the leaf layers in this very lesson were the example.
Math disagreements are settled with evidence and a test, not with politeness.
hints: Apply the same test to both flowers.
Does the definition say which direction the line must point?
If a mirror line exists, the symmetry exists.

stretch.prompt: A symmetric garden design puts the same planting on each side of a center path. One side uses 14 tulips and 9 daisies. How many flowers does the WHOLE symmetric design use?
stretch.explanation: One side uses 14 + 9 = 23 flowers, and the mirror side uses the same 23, so the whole design uses 23 × 2 = 46 flowers.
feedback: 23 is just ONE side — bilateral symmetry means the other side matches it, doubling the total.
28 doubles only the tulips (14 × 2) and forgets to double the 9 daisies.
126 multiplies 14 × 9 — but the two flower counts should be added, then doubled.
hints: First find the total for one side.
14 + 9 = 23 on one side.
A mirror image needs the same count on the other side.

stretch.prompt: You and a friend are studying a building for an art project. The building's left half mirrors its right half. What can you say about the building in terms of bilateral symmetry?
stretch.explanation: The building has bilateral symmetry: I can draw a vertical line of symmetry down its center, and every window, column, and door on the left is a mirror image of one on the right. The architects designed it that way on purpose — humans design for beauty using bilateral symmetry, because that balance is pleasing to our brains.
